title: WebSockets, SSE and long polling
subtitle: How a server can push live updates to apps, and how to pick between long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets.

c.v: A food delivery app adds live order tracking. When the restaurant marks an order as "cooking" or the rider moves, the phone should update at once. The team picks
and builds it in two weeks. On a laptop, it works well.

In production, two problems appear. First, many phones show "Reconnecting…" again and again. The team finds that their nginx proxy closes any connection that is quiet for 60 seconds. A cooking order can be quiet for ten minutes.

Second, some users never see "rider picked up". The team runs four WebSocket servers. The update is created on server 1, but the user's phone is connected to server 3. Server 1 has no idea that server 3 holds the user.
The fix takes another two weeks:

Normal HTTP is request and response. The client asks, and the server answers. The server cannot speak first. For live updates, like chat, scores or a rider on a map, you need the server to push.
There are four common ways to do this:

Pushing data means holding a connection open for every user. The hard part is not the protocol. It is keeping millions of open connections alive, routed and fed at the right speed.

Without HTTP/2, MDN says a browser allows only 6 SSE connections per domain, across all tabs. So a few open tabs can use them all up. Over HTTP/2, the browser and server agree on a stream limit, and the default is 100.

A WebSocket stays on the server where it started. Long polling sends many separate requests, so they need

One event must reach every user who cares, but those users sit on many servers. You put a
layer in the middle. Each server subscribes to the topics of its own users, and passes messages down their connections. Socket.IO calls this an adapter, and Redis is one option.
Slack does this at large scale. Gateway servers in many regions hold the users' WebSockets. A channel server, found by
, sends each message to every gateway with a subscriber. Each gateway then sends it to its own clients.
At Discord, each WebSocket gets its own session process. Anything published in a guild goes to every session connected to it.
A phone on a weak network reads slowly. If the server keeps sending, messages pile up in memory. MDN says the plain browser
interface has no backpressure. Fast messages can fill memory or use all the CPU.

Watch your server's queue per connection. When it grows too large, drop old updates, merge them, or close the connection and let the client resync.

Discord learned how slow parts spread. During peak hours, some guild processes could not keep up with their message queues. In another case, session processes grew their message queues until the whole Erlang VM ran out of memory.

q.v: Your app shows live sports scores. The browser only needs to receive updates. What is the simplest good fit?

options.v: Server-Sent Events, because data flows one way and the browser reconnects by itself.
WebSocket, because it is always faster.

why.v: SSE is one-way from server to client, and the EventSource API reconnects on its own with the Last-Event-ID header.

q.v: Your WebSocket connections behind nginx close after one quiet minute. What is a likely cause?

options.v: WebSockets cannot stay open longer than 60 seconds.
The proxy closes a connection when the server sends nothing for 60 seconds, which is the nginx default.
The browser limits each tab to one minute.

why.v: By default, nginx closes the connection if the proxied server sends no data for 60 seconds. Raise proxy_read_timeout, or have the server send ping frames.

q.v: You run 4 WebSocket servers. A user on server 3 does not get a message created on server 1. What is missing?

options.v: A pub/sub layer, so every server that holds a subscriber gets a copy of the message.

why.v: Each server only knows its own connections. Socket.IO calls this part an adapter, and Slack's channel servers do this job.

q.v: Why does long polling across many servers often need sticky sessions?

options.v: Each client sends many separate requests, and they must reach the server that holds its session.
Long polling encrypts data per server.

why.v: The Socket.IO docs say long polling sends many HTTP requests, so the load balancer must route each client to the same server.
